description: Three engineering students from Montevideo, Uruguay. Marcos Devincenzi, a pilot studying AI and Data Science, bridges aviation knowledge with technical expertise. Juan Benitez, in Systems Engineering, develops software for businesses and researches AI security. Facundo Díaz, also in AI and Data Science, leads the team’s modeling work.
summary:
Before the First Fire is a public, login-free dashboard that turns NASA combustion data into one practical question for lunar habitat engineers: which materials might burn differently on the Moon than in the Earth tests used to approve them?

The challenge suggests that microgravity and Earth results could bound what happens at lunar gravity. We tested that idea against the data. In the partial-gravity limits reproduced by Olson & Ferkul (2012, Table I), Mylar, Ultem and Nomex kept burning at lower oxygen in lunar gravity than in either microgravity or Earth gravity: for those materials, the bounds fail. And in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics tables for BASS-II and Saffire I–III, no solid sample was burned above 22.2% oxygen, while lunar cabins are planned at 30% or more.

The dashboard shows a flammability-versus-gravity curve, PSI coverage, material cards, an illustrative 3D flame chamber and "Ask the evidence", where an AI explains the closest NASA tests and code checks every citation. Before NASA's first fire experiment on the Moon (FM2), we registered three dated, falsifiable predictions that its results can confirm or refute.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Before the First Fire is a web dashboard for the engineers who choose materials and design ventilation for a lunar base. NASA screens spacecraft materials with flame tests in Earth gravity. Our dashboard shows what NASA's experiments say about lunar gravity, and where the evidence stops.

- Gravity curve: limiting oxygen for Mylar, Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 at microgravity, Moon, Mars and Earth gravity, with the planned habitat atmosphere as reference. Every point opens its platform, flow, pressure, source and page.

- NASA flight tests (PSI): which of our materials appear in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics tables, and at what oxygen. No solid sample in BASS-II or Saffire I–III was burned above 22.2% O2.

- Bounding the Moon: Saffire-II shows where microgravity and Earth agree; Olson & Ferkul (2012, Table I) show that for Mylar, Ultem and Nomex the lunar limit falls outside both.

- Ask the evidence: describe a material and a lunar cabin atmosphere in your own words. Code ranks the closest real tests by similarity of conditions (not risk) and says plainly when no test matches. Claude Haiku writes a short explanation from the retrieved records only; code verifies every cited ID and number, and falls back to a verified template if the check fails.

- FM2 predictions: three expectations for NASA's first fire experiment on the Moon, registered on 2026-11-14 at 22:26 (UTC-3), each with what would confirm or refute it.

- 3D flame chamber: an illustrative simulation comparing two gravities side by side, labeled as a simulation, not a measurement.

- Method page: the evidence, how answers are built, how we validated them, and the limits.

HOW IT WORKS

A structured catalogue of 229 NASA records (206 ranked) with value, unit, conditions, source and page for every number. Missing values say "not reported", never zero. Ranking runs in code with published weights. The AI cannot add records, numbers or claims of absence. 199 automated tests cover parsing, ranking and citation checks, and all 24 oxygen limits on the gravity curve match the paper's Table I.

BENEFITS

Lunar cabins are planned at 30% oxygen or more, beyond anything in the solid-fuel flight tests we reviewed. Showing exactly where the evidence stops tells engineers what must be tested before people live there. Our team in Uruguay sees the same question in Antarctica, where a 2012 fire spread through Brazil's Comandante Ferraz station, on the same island as Uruguay's Artigas base.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Most tools ask "what do we know?". Ours asks "what can we not yet assume?". We put gravity on the axis, tested the challenge's own suggestion that microgravity and Earth bound the Moon (for some materials they do not), and registered falsifiable predictions before NASA's experiment, so the dashboard can be proven wrong in public.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty first: every number links to its NASA source and page, simulations are labeled, and we never call a material "safe" or claim NASA "never tested" something, only what appears in the data we reviewed. The AI can explain but cannot invent: code checks its citations. The site is public, login-free, in English, works on phones, and keeps saved answers if the AI service is down.

TOOLS

JavaScript, TypeScript, React, Recharts, Zod, Vitest, Vite, Python, GitHub, Vercel, Anthropic API (Claude Haiku).
